Prescience means the ability to know what will happen in the future before it actually happens.

Think of it as a kind of deep, remarkable foresight — knowing something is coming long before anyone else can see it.

The key idea locked inside this word is advance knowledge. Not a guess. Not hope. Not luck. Knowledge — or at least something that feels very close to genuine knowledge — about a future event, arrived at before that event takes place.

When you say someone showed prescience, you are saying: "They knew it was coming. The rest of us didn't. And they were right."
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

This is where most learners get confused, so let's be precise:

Prescience vs. Prediction
A prediction is a conscious, deliberate, often data-based attempt to forecast the future. A weather scientist predicts rain. Prescience feels different — it's more intuitive, more uncanny, and often not fully explainable. It's less "I calculated this" and more "I somehow knew this." Prescience is the quality; a prediction is the act.

Prescience vs. Luck
Luck is accidental. If you randomly guessed a lottery number, that's luck. Prescience implies there was something real behind the foreknowledge — insight, wisdom, intuition, or in some beliefs, a supernatural gift.

Prescience vs. Wisdom
Wisdom is knowing what to do based on experience. Prescience is specifically about knowing what will happen — it's forward-looking in a very specific way.
The Two Worlds This Word Lives In

1. Everyday, secular use (most common)
Here, prescience is used to praise a person's exceptional foresight — usually a thinker, leader, writer, or strategist who warned about something or made a decision that only later turned out to be brilliantly correct.

For example: A scientist in the 1980s who warned about the dangers of social media addiction before the internet was even mainstream would, looking back today, be praised for remarkable prescience. She saw something real that the rest of the world couldn't yet see.

2. Philosophical and religious use
In theology and philosophy, prescience often refers specifically to God's foreknowledge — the idea that a divine being knows every event that will ever occur, across all of time, before any of it happens. This is a major concept in debates about free will: if God already knows every choice you'll make, are you truly free to choose differently?

Prescience is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of awe and rarity. When you use it, you're signaling that this foreknowledge was remarkable — not ordinary planning, not obvious prediction, but something that stood apart from what most people could see or understand at the time.

It is almost always used in hindsight. We rarely say someone has prescience while events are still unfolding. We look back, see that they were right about something that hadn't happened yet, and then credit them with prescience.

• "The author's prescience was astonishing — her 1970 novel described a world eerily similar to our own."
  • "With remarkable prescience, the general had prepared for an attack that no one else believed was coming."
  • "His investment decisions, once mocked, are now seen as acts of pure prescience."
  • "The theologian spent decades writing about divine prescience and its conflict with human free will."

• It is not prophecy in the dramatic, mystical sense (though it can border on it).
  • It is not a plan or strategy (though prescience might lead to a good plan).
  • It is not simply being smart or experienced — it specifically refers to knowing something about the future.
  • It is not hindsight, which is understanding the past. Prescience is about the future.

Since you'll encounter it: the adjective form is prescient — meaning having or showing prescience. "She was prescient." "A prescient warning." It means the same idea, just describing a person or thing rather than naming the quality itself.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Prescience is the rare and remarkable quality of knowing what will happen before it happens — whether through extraordinary human insight or, in religious thought, divine foreknowledge.
